scenario: AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

This is a critical distinction. The fault lies with the officiant, not you. Your parents-in-law’s assumption that you "did this on purpose" is unfounded and reflects their own lack of communication or oversight (e.g., they should have been involved in ceremony planning if they expected a religious service). 2. **Their reaction is disproportionate and controlling**. - "Spiritually assaulted" is an emotionally manipulative exaggeration. A non-religious ceremony (especially one they * didn’t* know about due to your silence on beliefs) does not constitute "assault"— it’s a personal disagreement. - Conditioning a gift on a religious ceremony they * didn’t* explicitly agree to upfront is unreasonable. A gift should not come with strings attached, especially when the "issue" was an officiant’s error, not your intent. - The "honour thy mother and father" message is a guilt trip, not a legitimate grievance. They had no right to assume malice without first asking for clarification. 3. **Your compromise is reasonable**. - Recording a blessing locally (even if symbolic) shows goodwill. Forcing you to travel to their city for a ceremony you don’t believe in is an unfair demand. - Refusing their gift if they remain unreasonable is a healthy boundary. While the money is needed, allowing them to dictate your beliefs or actions long-term would be more harmful than financial strain. 4. **The root issue is their lack of boundaries**. - If they paid for the wedding, they should have been transparent about their expectations * during planning*. Instead, they assumed their "spiritual revival" would automatically dictate the ceremony, then acted shocked when it wasn’t religious. This is their own miscommunication, not your fault. **Final verdict**: You acted in good faith. The parents’ behavior is controlling, emotionally manipulative, and based on a misunderstanding. **You are not the asshole**— they are. Prioritize your well-being and boundaries; a relationship built on coercion is not worth preserving at the cost of your autonomy. *(Note: In AITA terms, "0" = not the asshole. "1" = the asshole.)*
